objectives: Explain how a dictionary attack differs from trying every possible password
Analyse a login request in the browser and turn it into an ffuf command
Separate failed from successful attempts by response size or content
Describe how the CybICS IDS detects login guessing and which defences stop it
takeaways: A dictionary attack tries passwords people really use, which is why weak and default passwords fall quickly.
Study one failed login by hand first: the URL, the body format and what a failure looks like.
ffuf replaces FUZZ with each wordlist entry, and a filter on size or text hides the failures.
Many failed logins from one source are noisy; the CybICS IDS alerts on five within thirty seconds.
Changing default passwords and limiting who can reach a login stop most attacks; lockouts need care in OT.

checkpoints.question: Every wrong password returns an answer of exactly 4561 bytes. Which ffuf option hides those answers?
checkpoints.explanation: -fs filters out responses of a given size, so only answers that differ remain. -ms does the opposite: it matches that size and would show you only the failures. -fc filters by HTTP status code, and 4561 is not a status code.

quiz.question: Why is a dictionary attack usually much faster than trying every possible password?
options: It sends many login requests in parallel
It tries the passwords people really choose
It reads the password hash from the server first
It tries short passwords first, then longer ones
quiz.explanation: Real passwords are not random. Lists from past breaches contain the passwords people pick, so a weak one is found among the first entries. Parallel requests help any attack but do not explain the difference, and trying short passwords first is still trying every possible password, just in a different order.

quiz.question: The OpenPLC login sends a form and the FUXA login sends JSON to an API. What do you have to change in your ffuf command when you switch targets?
options: Nothing; ffuf detects the login format itself
URL, Content-Type, body format and likely the filter
Only the wordlist, since FUXA users differ
Only the URL and port; the -fs filter stays valid for both
quiz.explanation: ffuf sends exactly what you tell it. A different login means a different URL, a different body and a different failure answer, so the filter that worked for one target may not work for the other. The FUXA failure answer is not the size of the OpenPLC one.

quiz.question: What does MITRE ATT&CK for ICS technique T1694.001 describe?
options: Guessing passwords from a breach wordlist
Logging in with a device's factory login
Using any stolen or guessed login
Sniffing passwords off the network
quiz.explanation: T1694.001 Default Credentials covers logins that are the same on every unit and documented by the vendor. A wordlist attack can find such a login, but guessing is not what the technique describes, and using any login that works, stolen or guessed, is T0859 Valid Accounts.

quiz.question: An attacker sends one guess every ten seconds. Does the CybICS http_brute_force rule fire?
options: Yes, every failed login raises an alert
No, it reaches only three in thirty seconds
Yes, because it comes from the attack machine
No, because the IDS does not watch port 8080
quiz.explanation: It is a rate rule: five attempts in a thirty-second window from one source, and it does watch ports 8080 and 1881. A slow attacker stays below it, which is why defenders also review failed-login logs over longer periods.

quiz.question: Which measures help against password attacks on an HMI? (Select all that apply)
options: Replacing default passwords with long, unique ones
Making the login reachable only from the control network
Adding growing delays after failed attempts
Hiding the login page behind a different URL and changing nothing else
quiz.explanation: Strong passwords make guessing fail, segmentation limits who can try, and delays make large wordlists impractical. A hidden URL is found quickly by anyone who scans or watches traffic.
